item.title: Introducing Claude Meetings
item.abstract: Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta. Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission. Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab) , or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to. Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon. What it looks like Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking. When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc. Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab) . Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai. We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, and Otter so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses. Security and privacy Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page. By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript. Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call. When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio. Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed. Getting started Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027. Setup steps are in the Help Center .

item.title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB , a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) , and AWS X-Ray , a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: Figure 1: Architecture of Natera’s SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team’s first architectural decision was where to run the agents. The team required a managed runtime that would handle container orchestration, scaling, and security without requiring them to maintain custom infrastructure. They chose AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts both swarm-agent and swarm-hive in a secure, managed environment with built-in identity management and monitoring, avoiding the need to build and operate a custom agent execution layer. You can adopt this pattern regardless of the framework you choose. The team chose a keyless deployment model because SWARM runs in a clinical environment where credentials exposure is unacceptable. OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) generate temporary credentials scoped per deployment, with no long-lived keys in the pipeline. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforces least privilege at the component level. Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) with private subnets and VPC endpoints keeps traffic off the public internet. AWS Secrets Manager rotates the few credentials that exist on an automatic 30-day cycle. GitLab CI runners authenticate to AWS by presenting an OIDC token to an IAM identity provider configured in the account. AWS STS exchanges the token for short-lived credentials scoped to the deployment role (no long-lived access keys are stored in the pipeline). For setup details, see the IAM OIDC provider documentation . The following example illustrates the pattern: an IAM OIDC trust policy for GitLab CI follows this structure: These infrastructure-level security controls work in concert with SWARM’s data governance policies. Together they form the full compliance posture required for operating an AI system in a regulated clinical environment. SWARM runs on HIPAA-eligible AWS services under a Business Associate Agreement ( BAA ), reflecting Natera’s obligations as a clinical laboratory operator. Every agent invocation is audit-logged (a searchable record that satisfies data access traceability requirements). No patient-identifiable information touches the vector index or the language model. Tickets contain only equipment and workflow metadata. Teams building under HIPAA or similar regulatory frameworks should confirm BAA coverage and data separation requirements before designing the knowledge base pipeline. Early prototypes using general-purpose retrieval without equipment-specific metadata produced inconsistent results, so the Natera team built a custom document processing pipeline tailored to technical equipment documentation. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings generates vector representations for semantic search, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), converting documents into embeddings stored in batches of 100, a size chosen to balance indexing throughput against API rate limits. For heavily structured source documents with tables and diagrams, investing in a custom parsing pipeline rather than relying on default chunking compounds accuracy gains across every diagnosis. Amazon Bedrock services, including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are available in multiple AWS Regions. For the latest information, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supported Regions . The Natera team uses the tiktoken tokenizer with the cl100k_base encoding to measure chunk boundaries. The following example illustrates the pattern, the chunking configuration follows a standard structure: For more on batch ingestion patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation . “Diagnostic accuracy is a data quality problem first,” Jirau said. “Adding missing vendor manuals for the lowest-scoring instrument family lifted accuracy from 71% to 75% with no model changes.” This shaped the Natera team’s improvement approach: when accuracy plateaus, the team checks data coverage before model tuning, because gaps in vendor documentation are the most common cause of missed diagnoses. The pipeline reprocesses new or updated documents and refreshes the vector index without disrupting active operations. The Natera team faced a key architectural choice: embed logic directly in agent prompts, or build a separate, versioned skill library. Natera chose the library approach because it makes SWARM auditable and improvable. “When a diagnosis is wrong, we need to point to a specific skill rather than debug the whole system — that’s why we built a versioned skill library from the start,” Jirau said. The library contains 33 skills: 24 instrument-specific skills covering the full range of equipment families Natera supports, plus 9 cross-cutting workflow skills that apply broadly across ticket types.

item.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
item.abstract: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

item.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
item.abstract:
🤏 smolmaxxing Run the biggest language model you can on the smallest hardware you own. TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself. Two devices so far 📺 Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) 📱 iPad Air (2013) Chip Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 Apple A7, 2 cores RAM 1.9 GB (about 1 GB usable) 1 GB (about 700 MB usable) OS Android 14, no root iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken Everyday model Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s Biggest model Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 5.1 tok/s Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 2.6-4.5 tok/s Full results docs/tv-box.md ipad-air/README.md Both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash as it's needed. More devices (phones, single-board computers, routers) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM. How it works All of it is a patch on llama.cpp . The main ideas: Kernels built for the chip. A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions. Less RAM per model. Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Experts paged from flash. A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB. Streaming for dense models bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed. docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its measured gain. Try it The quickest start is a ready-made model file from Hugging Face. They need the patched llama.cpp: stock llama.cpp can't load them. TV box or another ARMv8.2 Android device: docs/tv-box-setup.md Jailbroken iPad on iOS 12: ipad-air/README.md All model files and how to rebuild them: docs/models.md Read more Page What's in it docs/tv-box.md device #1: every model run on the TV box, speed and quality ipad-air/README.md device #2: the iPad Air results, setup and scripts docs/how-it-works.md the kernels, memory tricks, expert pager and streaming engine docs/models.md downloads for both devices, rebuild targets and checksums docs/lessons.md what we learned, including what didn't work EXPERIMENT.md the full lab notebook: 160 experiments, failures included What's in the repo Path What patches/ every change to llama.cpp for the TV box (the iPad's patch is in ipad-air/patches/ ) tools/ model rebuilding, GGUF rewriting, benchmarks and kernel checks tv-llm-ui/ the live token-stream chat page and its launcher ipad-air/ device #2: iOS 12 build, smolchat , deploy and benchmark scripts bench/ every chat benchmark ( results.jsonl ) and the raw logs data/ vocabulary lists and evaluation texts tiny-llm-web/ the first experiment: a 260K-parameter story model zigcc/ zig wrappers for cross-compiling static aarch64 binaries Star History License MIT . The llama.cpp patches are derivatives of llama.cpp (MIT). Model weights keep their own licenses, and the evaluation texts are Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0). Models from Qwen , unsloth (GGUFs and importance matrices), PrismML (Bonsai), inclusionAI (Ling-mini-2.0), tablinum (Moon-Beam), bartowski and mradermacher (GGUFs), Google (Gemma) and stories260K . The iPad is jailbroken with Amethyst . The banner uses Archivo (SIL OFL) and is rendered by tools/banner/render.sh . The 🤏 logo is the pinching-hand emoji from Google's Noto Emoji (Apache 2.0).

item.title: 馬斯克Grok洩露自家機密！SpaceX特斯拉工資績效全曝光
item.abstract: 馬斯克Grok洩露自家機密！SpaceX特斯拉工資績效全曝光 henry 2026-11-12 18:08:24 來源： 量子位 Grok在讓人破繃這件事上，從來不會讓人失望。 henry 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI Grok在讓人破繃這件事上，從來不會讓人失望。 就在剛剛，安全公司Claroc發現， 超過3.5萬個用Grok構建的應用，無需登入就能訪問，其中一部分直接暴露了企業機密和個人隱私。 最扎眼的是，老馬自家的SpaceXSI（SpaceX與xAI合併後的公司）和X，也在其中。 員工入職計劃、銷售客戶資料、廣告提案……連自家的底兒，都被抖出來了。 而且，沒合併的特斯拉也沒躲過去。一份服務中心評分表，把22名技術人員的姓名、工作效率和獎金情況擺到了公開網頁上。 更騷的是，不光是用自己產品的自家員工遭了殃，洩露內容還涉及普通人的敏感資訊。 包括，ICU患者的化驗結果、影像檢查、呼吸機使用記錄，以及企業員工的明文賬戶密碼。 我勒個豆，真就用Grok，免費送一鍵開盒嗎？ 到底洩露了什麼？ 具體來說，在事情的一開始，Claroc測試了43551個（37571個仍然線上）Grok Build應用地址，發現94.7%的線上應用無需登入就能開啟。 雖說這些應用大多都是你我製作的AI泔水，像什麼小遊戲，計算器之類的…… 但沙裡淘金，經過模型篩查和人工抽樣，Claroc估計，其中大概有650—800個應用包含私密資料。 涉及的機構包括SpaceXSI、X，以及另外30家企業，其中6家入選《財富》500強。 這些資料有多敏感呢，舉幾個例子你就知道了： 1、一份ICU患者簡報，包含患者化驗結果、影像檢查和呼吸機使用狀態。 2、一家承包商的工時管理應用，把18個賬戶的明文密碼寫進了指令碼，訪問頁面的人都可以下載。 3、SpaceXSI的內部銷售工具，包含戰略客戶賬戶、銷售商機和內部團隊資訊。 4、特斯拉服務中心評分表，包含員工姓名、工作效率和獎金情況。 。。。。 看下來，雖然真有「誰家好人」在Vibe Coding上的東西，記錄自己的密碼，以及體檢報告。 但Grok這傢伙直接給人公之於眾了，也實在過於逆天。 那麼，這些本來應該只在公司內部流轉的資料，怎麼會出現在公開網頁上？ 一個隨機連結，怎麼就成了開盒入口？ 簡單來說，在你用Grok vibecoding時，它會為每個釋出的應用分配一個獨立網址，形式類似於隨機名稱.grok.me。 這些隨機名稱由幾個單片語成，設計初衷就是讓別人難以猜中。但問題在於， 網址難猜，不代表訪問許可權安全。 Claroc發現，這些應用地址可以通過被動DNS（Passive DNS）資料庫批次找到。 簡單來說，每當有人訪問一個網站，計算機都需要通過DNS查詢域名對應的伺服器地址。部分DNS解析服務會收集這些查詢記錄，並將其放進可搜尋的資料庫。 於是，一條發現路徑就形成了： 有人訪問應用 → DNS查詢留下記錄 → 域名進入被動DNS資料庫 → 外部人員批次找到應用地址。 如果應用的訪問許可權設定為「任何持有連結的人」，那麼只要找到網址，就能直接開啟。 也就是說，Grok用隨機網址增加了應用被發現的難度，卻沒有真正解決訪問控制問題。 為了公平起見，Claroc還拿ChatGPT應用做了對照測試：其應用地址同樣可能被被動DNS收錄，但分享面板預設設定為「僅限我」。即使別人找到了網址，也無法訪問。 此乃ChatGPT一勝！ 此外，為了驗證Grok生成的程式碼是否可靠以及如何處理團隊許可權。 Claroc後面還用虛構資料，自行搭建了一個供四人銷售團隊使用的客戶管理應用。 雖說Grok確實自動添加了Google和X登入功能，但研究人員檢查程式碼後發現了一個低階錯誤： 應用先把登入者加入團隊，再檢查他是不是團隊成員。也就是先拉你進群，再看是不是群友。 那肯定都是群友啦…… 隨後，研究人員使用一個從未受到邀請的Google賬戶登入，結果不僅看到了全部客戶資料，還成功修改了一條記錄、刪除了另一條記錄。 也就是說，只要你想，Grokd的大門永遠為你敞開。 官方回應與後續 事情曝光後，SpaceXSI向媒體表示，應用在建立者主動分享前都是私密的，釋出需要經過多個步驟。 公司還稱，其員工賬戶預設設定為「僅限你」，要公開應用，需要主動修改許可權。 但Claroc表示，在其用於測試的付費賬戶中，釋出面板預先選中的，卻是「任何持有連結的人」。 這裡的關鍵在於： 釋出前私密，和釋出時預設讓誰訪問，是兩道題。 如果一路點完「釋出」，最終預選的訪問範圍仍然是所有持有連結的人，多確認幾次，也不會自動補上一份團隊成員名單。 研究人員也驗證了Grok現有的許可權控制功能。 切換為「僅限你」後，陌生人訪問頁面和資料介面，都會被拒絕；取消釋出，也能在幾秒內讓應用下線。 所以，Grok有能用的保護措施。問題在於，使用者把內部工具釋出出去時，這些措施有沒有真正用上。 目前，這事兒已經在推特吵起來了，有人認為是人自己開的許可權，也有人認為是Grok的許可權設定有問題。 至於後續的處理嘛，直到Ars Technica發出採訪郵件後的數小時內，SpaceXSI才開始移除相關連結。 截至報道釋出，24個由SpaceXSI和X員工建立的應用已經全部下線。 但其他使用者建立的大量應用仍然可以訪問，Claroc也已開始自行聯絡受影響機構。 至於平臺是否會主動通知其他受影響客戶，Ars Technica也尚未得到明確答覆。 參考連結 item.title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
item.abstract: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write. AWS describes cache entries as scoped to your account and Region, not to your tenants. In a multi-tenant application, prepend a tenant-specific SHA-256 hash to the cacheable prefix. The Optimizing cost and latency with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for Anthropic models post describes this pattern. Enforce tenant authorization before you build the prompt.
